description: We are Team Odyssey & Orbit, five students from Bangladesh who love space and storytelling. Tafim leads the team and the research, Rana builds the website and its design, Rifat checks every NASA fact and photo, Arman creates our videos and visuals, and Nowrin writes the stories and gives them her voice. Together we turned NASA's forgotten machines into friendly storytellers, so every child can meet them, learn real science and dream big.
summary: Abandoned, but not Forgotten is an interactive storytelling website, built by Team Odyssey & Orbit from Bangladesh, where the machines NASA left on the Moon and Mars tell their own stories to school-age kids. A child picks Surveyor 3, the Apollo 17 Lunar Roving Vehicle, Opportunity or Ingenuity, and the machine greets them as a friendly 3D character and narrates its journey with voice and captions: why it was built, how it got there, what it discovered and where it rests today. The challenge notes that young space fans often hear only about active missions, so we turn NASA's historical record into a story a child wants to follow. Every fact sits on a "NASA DATA" card with its source linked, every photo is a real NASA image linked to NASA's website, and a built-in NASA Archive searches NASA's Image and Video Library live. It runs in any browser on a phone, tablet or laptop with nothing to install, so children everywhere can learn real science from NASA's own data and see that these machines are not forgotten.
details:
Abandoned, but not Forgotten is an interactive, narrated 3D story website by Team Odyssey & Orbit. Four machines that humans left behind on the Moon and Mars tell their own stories to school-age children: Surveyor 3 (1967) and the Apollo 17 Lunar Roving Vehicle (1972) on the Moon, Opportunity (2004–2018) and Ingenuity (2021–2024) on Mars.

What it does and how it works

A child opens the website, taps "Start Exploring" and picks a machine on the Moon or Mars. The machine appears as a friendly 3D cartoon explorer, says hello and tells its story in the first person, with a voice and on-screen captions. Each story has the same journey: a flashback to why the machine was built and how it travelled, a 3D globe showing where it landed, a 3D surface scene of where it rests today, a route map of its journey, and achievements unlocked with real NASA photos. Every fact appears on a "NASA DATA" card with a link to its NASA source, and every photo links to its page on NASA's website. When a story ends, the child can replay it or go on to the next machine. The stories run in order from the Moon to Mars and finish in our NASA Archive, a live search of the NASA Image and Video Library, where children can look up any machine, mission or place and open real photos on NASA's site.

Benefits and intended impact

The challenge points out that school-age space fans often hear only about active, ongoing missions. Our project gives the older, silent machines a voice, so children learn what they were, why they were sent and what science they made possible. Because it runs in any web browser on a phone, tablet or laptop with nothing to install, any child with a link can use it, at home or in a classroom. Next, we want to bring it to classrooms, add more machines and offer it in children's own languages, starting with Bangla.

Tools and technologies

• HTML5, CSS3 and plain JavaScript (single-page app, no framework) • three.js (WebGL) for the 3D machines, globes and surface scenes • Web Speech API for narration, with captions on screen • Canvas 2D for maps and illustrations made in code • NASA Images API (images-api.nasa.gov) for live archive search • Python for the build script that generates the Moon story pages • GitHub Pages for hosting; open source under Apache-2.0

How it is creative

Instead of a textbook page, each machine is the storyteller: a talking character with its own personality who takes the child back in time and then shows where it is today. The story is told like a game, with a journey map and achievements to unlock, but every unlock is a real NASA fact or photo.

Factors we considered

• Accuracy: facts come from NASA mission pages and the NASA Image and Video Library, and each one shows its source. Illustrations made in code (globes, maps, 3D models) are clearly labelled as illustrations, never presented as real photos. • Age-appropriate language: short, friendly sentences for children, with captions for every line. • Access: works on low-cost phones and any modern browser, with nothing to install; children can skip ahead or take manual control. • Respect for sources: NASA, JPL-Caltech and other credits are shown on every photo.
